Ghost RiversSwift River case studyResearch mapField guide

By Paul Shoemaker · October 27, 2026

The Swift River, Maine

Searching for the Waterways That Came Before

The first Ghost Rivers case study begins around Byron and Coos Canyon in western Maine. The question is not simply where the river flows now. It is which older deposits can actually be documented, how they formed, and what remains unknown about their gold content.

Our strongest initial finding: published geological mapping identifies older valley gravels reworked from glacial deposits, alongside glacial meltwater features in the surrounding study area. That supports investigating an older landscape. It does not establish a buried pay channel.

Open the interactive research map · Take the field-analysis guide

First, make sure it is the right Swift River

This is the Swift River in western Maine, around Byron, not the Swift River in New Hampshire's Saco watershed. The prototype uses a rectangular study window covering parts of the Ellis Pond and Roxbury quadrangles. It includes neighboring drainage areas; it is not a delineated Swift River watershed boundary. A feature inside that rectangle does not automatically belong to the Swift River's former drainage.

Bedrock gives the canyon its structure

Robert G. Marvinney's 2008 Maine Geological Survey circular identifies the canyon's bedrock as the Perry Mountain Formation, with alternating quartzite and schist. His photographs illustrate differential weathering, folds, and erosion potholes. These are documented geological features; they are not measurements of gold in the cracks. Read Marvinney's Coos Canyon publication record and the illustrated circular, pages 3–10.

The original sedimentary structures preserved in metamorphic rock record a much older geological history. They should not be mistaken for the bed of a recently abandoned Swift River channel. For wider bedrock context, Robert H. Moench and Carol T. Hildreth published the 1976 Rumford quadrangle map, GQ-1272; it is a regional bedrock reference, not a sediment-thickness or gold-grade map.

The survey maps an older sediment landscape

Lindsay J. Spigel's Ellis Pond map, 21-8 (2021), and Roxbury map, 20-3 (2020), provide the local surficial mapping used in this prototype. We inspected their publication records and the unit descriptions and geometries in the MGS 1:24,000 digital service. Full map-sheet interpretation and field verification remain future work.

The digital explanations distinguish:

  • Reworked valley deposits, Qst: sand and gravel produced by rivers reworking glacial deposits. The explanation names the Swift River among several valleys and says most of these mapped deposits are abandoned by modern stream processes. This is stronger evidence than guessing from elevation alone.
  • Modern stream alluvium, Ha: floodplain sediment. It can overlap older deposits, so the surface category does not reveal the whole vertical sequence.
  • Till, Pt: poorly sorted material deposited by ice, potentially including lenses of water-laid sediment. Compact till is not automatically solid bedrock or a pay layer.
  • Ice-contact and meltwater deposits: separate map units address ice-contact gravel, subglacial meltwater deposits, and glacial lake sediments. They should not all be renamed ancient river gravel.

The queried study window contains 138 mapped sediment/bedrock-exposure polygons and 72 published meltwater-channel centerline features. These are database feature counts, not 138 targets or 72 distinct ancient rivers. Geometries have been simplified for display. Click a feature to see its unit or symbol, quadrangle, original source, and limits.

What the meltwater lines do—and do not—show

The survey's line explanation interprets channels eroded by glacial meltwater and notes that most were delineated using LiDAR topography. Those lines are attributed survey interpretations, not routes drawn by Gold Trails. Their age is described only broadly as glacial/deglacial; we have not independently dated them.

The prototype does not reproduce the original flow arrows. Consult the published map before drawing conclusions about flow direction or connections between segments. No gold assay or grade is attached to a meltwater line.

Three hypotheses to test

H1 — Reworked terrace contacts could retain gold. The mapped Qst deposits provide a geological reason to ask the question. Whether their basal contacts contain recoverable gold remains unverified. No terrace has been ranked as a prospecting destination.

H2 — Later streams could reconcentrate older glacial sediment. The Maine Geological Survey's gold overview describes bedrock, glacial sediment, and stream deposits as different settings for Maine gold, and lists the Byron-area Swift River among reported gold-bearing streams. That regional occurrence does not identify which local layer supplied a pan.

H3 — A terrain hollow might be an abandoned channel. A shape alone is insufficient. We need mapped sediment relationships, dated imagery, or field evidence to distinguish a recent cutoff from a meltwater channel, a drainage ditch, or another landform. No new hypothetical channel has been drawn on the map.

Creator observations: useful comparisons, with limits

Our existing library contains eight Coos Canyon/Swift River video records, but no imported timestamped findings linked to those eight sources. Local transcript review is therefore a real research gap. Video titles are not evidence that an ancient channel was identified.

For a general comparison, imported caption notes for Ask Jeff Williams discuss a proposed elevated channel remnant in a different region. Watch the recorded anchor at 1:30. It is an example of a question to investigate, not corroboration for a Maine terrace.

Imported notes for Minerals, Rocks, and Fossil Talks compare till with water-laid deposits. See the recorded anchor at 0:55. Sorting and layering can inform an interpretation, but appearance does not settle age or gold content. These links preserve caption-derived anchors; their audio and footage have not been independently reviewed. Neither creator is presented as having demonstrated a Swift River paleochannel.

What we have not established

We have not documented a dated historical shift in the active Swift River alignment, completed a historical aerial-photo comparison, measured terrace heights above the modern stream, established buried gravel thickness, or demonstrated gold-bearing basal contacts. Nor have we located and evaluated the original historical production records sufficiently to publish a local production total.

The next useful work is a controlled comparison: choose dated images and matching map editions, verify the mapped deposit, record an elevation profile with its datum and uncertainty, and seek permission before considering any sampling. See the field guide for a low-impact starting routine.

Sources checked October 27, 2026. Source publication years and the scope of inspection are stated above. Research interpretations are provisional; no site access is granted by this case study.
